reasons.D: Closest movement and stance: short, jaunty sentences opening on 'And', a chatty first-person 'I set this down plainly' for the natives, teasing asides about locals who can't find it, and piled-up lists that echo the author's cataloguing rhythm.
reasons.C: Has the author's wry, conversational irony, parenthetical asides and punchy short sentences ('Nothing is grand. Everything is right.'), but it is smoother and more polished-Edwardian than the author's colloquial, fragmentary bounce.
reasons.B: Uses the first person and a genteel humour, but the long, balanced sentences and the extended gentlewoman simile make it more formal and measured than the author's exclamatory, slangy manner.
reasons.A: Plain modern expository prose with even sentence lengths, no first person, no exclamation or colloquialism; it is the furthest from the author's playful, fragmentary voice.
